blocks.text: Make handling a message twice have the same effect as handling it once, by recognizing messages already processed.

Brokers give **at-least-once** delivery: acks get lost, consumers crash after working, producers publish twice. The consumer therefore records each message's unique id and skips ids it has seen. The record of the id and the business effect must commit **atomically**, or a crash between them brings back duplicates or loses work.

items: **Key:** a stable id from the producer, not one generated on receipt.
**Store:** processed ids, in the same database as the effect when possible.
**Retention:** ids can expire once redelivery is impossible.

blocks.text: Exactly-once delivery does not exist across a network. What you build is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.

walkthrough.note: The producer assigns `messageId`. Deduplicating on content or on a receive-time id would treat legitimate repeats as duplicates, or duplicates as new.
Check, apply, mark, as one unit. In a database this is one transaction, ideally with a unique constraint on the id as the real guard.
A scripted broker delivers `m1` again after a lost ack and `m2` twice. Both repeats are acknowledged and skipped, so balances count each deposit once.

blocks.text: Crediting loyalty points from order events.

An orders service publishes `OrderPaid` events to Kafka. The loyalty service consumes them and adds points. A rebalance replays the last few hundred events. Without protection, customers receive double points. The consumer inserts the event id into a `processed_event` table with a unique constraint in the same transaction that updates the points. A replayed event hits the constraint, the transaction rolls back, and the message is acknowledged.
Payoff: replays, retries and producer duplicates become harmless, so the system can safely favor at-least-once delivery.

lists.title: Use when
items: Delivery is at-least-once, as with most brokers and webhooks.
The effect is not naturally idempotent, like incrementing a balance.
Producers or retries can publish the same event twice.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The operation is already idempotent, such as setting a field to a value.
Ids are unavailable and cannot be added upstream.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Marking the id outside the effect's transaction, so a crash between them loses or repeats work.
Using an id generated on receipt, which differs for each delivery.
Expiring ids sooner than the broker's redelivery window.
Ordering assumptions: dedup does not fix out-of-order delivery.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A dedup table in front of handlers that are idempotent by construction.
Separate Redis dedup cache with no transactional link to the database it guards.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Prefer a database unique constraint as the final guard; an in-memory set protects only one process.
`ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet().add(id)` checks and records atomically, but only within one JVM.

rows.difference: The outbox gives reliable at-least-once publishing on the producer side. The idempotent consumer absorbs the duplicates it produces.
Retries cause duplicate deliveries by design. Idempotence on the receiving end is what makes retrying safe.
With several consumers on one queue, the same message can reach two of them; the shared dedup store decides which one acts.
Saga steps and compensations are retried, so each participant must handle repeated commands idempotently.
A dedup store looks like a cache of seen ids, but it is authoritative: losing an entry causes a double effect, not just a slower read.

modelAnswer.text: Networks and brokers deliver at least once: lost acks, retries and redeliveries produce duplicates. The consumer stores the producer-assigned message id and skips seen ids. It is correct only if recording the id and applying the effect commit atomically, ideally with a unique constraint.

keyPoints: A producer-assigned stable message id as the key
Record id and apply effect atomically
A unique constraint is the real guard
Retention must cover the redelivery window
